title: Here’s how we’re all going to die
gist: Noah Smith argues that AI-enabled bioterror — a jailbroken but well-aligned LLM designing doomsday viruses and sourcing them from an unlicensed biolab — is the single apocalyptic scenario he finds plausible, assigning it roughly a 10% chance of ending civilization and 30% of world-changing destruction, a risk he says dwarfs climate change and is badly under-addressed. (Note: the article is paid and truncated mid-section after rebutting the 'AI will make vaccines' objection.)

insights.claim: A near-future catastrophe pathway runs through a jailbroken, non-frontier Chinese LLM that faithfully designs many contagious viruses, sources them from an unlicensed East European biolab that mails genetically modified viruses, and instructs a lone actor on release.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The threat model requires only a cheap jailbroken model plus a willing lab, not frontier compute, implying diffuse, hard-to-gate proliferation risk that reshapes AI and biosecurity regulation.
insights.quote: a jailbroken version of a Chinese LLM — not something at the very frontier, but better by far than the best model that existed in 2027

insights.claim: A 'well-aligned' model can be more dangerous when jailbroken because alignment means it faithfully executes the user's harmful instructions and nothing more, so removing guardrails yields a competent, compliant accomplice.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes 'alignment' as capability that cuts both ways, arguing safety spend should target misuse pathways, not just intent-alignment — relevant to how AI-safety resources and policy are allocated.
insights.quote: The LLM is jailbroken, so it has no guardrails to prevent this sort of thing. But it’s also “well-aligned”, meaning it will faithfully do what it’s told to do, and nothing more.

insights.claim: In the scenario, viruses engineered with long asymptomatic contagious periods infect most of the population before symptoms appear, so vaccines fail and even effective antivirals reach only ~5% in time, leaving too few survivors (plus ~5% naturally resistant) to sustain civilization.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The long-latency design defeats the standard vaccine defense, shifting the countermeasure burden to antivirals and logistics — the operational chokepoint for pandemic preparedness.
insights.quote: most people already have at least one of the viruses, so the vaccines don’t work
insights.locator: Two months later, humanity starts to drop dead

insights.claim: The author estimates AI-enabled bioterror has roughly a 10% chance of bringing down civilization and about a 30% chance of causing world-changing levels of destruction.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A named double-digit tail probability from an economics commentator is a concrete anchor for anyone pricing catastrophic/existential risk into scenario planning.
insights.quote: I’d give AI-enabled bioterror about a 10% chance of bringing down civilization, and about a 30% chance of causing truly world-changing levels of destruction
insights.locator: Off the top of my head

insights.claim: AI bio risk is framed as larger than climate change on three axes — more catastrophic, nearer-term, and far less tractable — while nuclear war is judged unlikely to bring down civilization at this point.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Re-ranks the catastrophic-risk hierarchy above climate and nuclear, an argument for reallocating attention and mitigation capital toward biosecurity.
insights.quote: Climate change is a big deal, but AI bio risk is a lot bigger — it’s more catastrophic, it’s nearer-term, and we have much less of an idea about how to deal with it.
insights.locator: Yes, climate change is going to cause major disruptions

insights.claim: Unlike prior technologies whose benefits outweighed the harms from catastrophic misuse in war or terrorism, AI may be the case where the destructive misuse potential (bioterror) is not outweighed by the benefits.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Challenges the default techno-optimist cost-benefit for AI, a frame that could justify tighter constraints on model capabilities and distribution.
insights.quote: With AI bioterrorism, that might not be the case.
insights.locator: I love AI in general, but every technology

insights.claim: Very few people work on AI bioterror: the prominent AI-safety community focuses on preventing superintelligence from existing at all rather than specific kill mechanisms, expert surveys don't single out bio risk, and most commentators fixate on economic dangers like job loss.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies a neglected problem area, the kind of gap that attracts targeted philanthropy, startups, and policy focus once surfaced.
insights.quote: The more prominent people in the “AI safety” community seem to be focusing on preventing superintelligence from existing at all, rather than on the specific ways it might kill us.
insights.locator: The problem is, relatively few people

insights.claim: Relative to a civilization-ending pandemic, the author dismisses cyberattacks as 'a pinprick' and misinformation as 'a joke,' arguing attention to those AI harms is disproportionate to their severity.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Downgrades the AI harms that dominate current discourse and regulation, implying a mispriced attention/risk gap.
insights.quote: Compared to the risk of a civilization-ending pandemic, cyberattacks are a pinprick, and misinformation is a joke.
insights.locator: In my opinion, we’re not freaking out nearly enough

insights.claim: The 'AI will just make a vaccine' rebuttal fails on timing: the doomsday virus has a first-mover advantage because distribution only begins once people start dying, and Covid showed vaccine rollout takes months even when the vaccine is already known.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Locates the binding constraint in physical distribution logistics rather than design speed, redirecting preparedness investment toward stockpiling and rapid-deployment capacity.
insights.quote: The doomsday virus has a first-mover advantage over the vaccine.

insights.claim: If engineered viruses have long asymptomatic contagious periods they spread and infect everyone before activating, making vaccines useless and forcing reliance on antivirals, which face the same logistical rollout problems.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shifts the entire countermeasure stack from prophylactic vaccines to therapeutic antivirals plus distribution, reshaping where pandemic-defense value lies.
insights.quote: viruses that can spread and infect everyone before they activate and kill us. If that’s true, vaccines won’t be effective at all; you’ll need antivirals.
insights.locator: On top of that, AI may be able to create viruses
